title_original: 【関西プレビュー】「住友春翠ー仕合せの住友近代美術コレクション」泉屋博古館で10月31日から12月20日まで　住友家十五代当主の美意識をひもとく充実の特別展
editorial_title_zh: 【关西预览】“住友春翠—美满的住友近代美术收藏”泉屋博古馆将于10月31日至12月20日举办　一场深入诠释住友家第十五代当主美学意识的丰富特展

true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "泉屋博古馆（京都市）将从10月31日至12月20日举办特展“逝世100周年纪念 住友春翠—美满的住友近代美术收藏”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当作品被纳为收藏时，每一件都拥有各自的故事。这就是“何时、何地、谁、什么、为何以及如何”获得——住友收藏涵盖了中国古代青铜器、中国及日本书画、西洋绘画、近代陶瓷器、茶具、文房具，甚至还包括面具及戏服等广泛领域，其中大部分是由为当前住友集团奠定基础的住友家第15代当主住友吉左卫门友纯（号：春翠，1864～1926）在明治中期至大正时代购入的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "曾造访须磨别邸的洋画家小杉未醒对春翠的印象做出了这样的评价：“富豪具有双重人格，一个是富豪其人的人格，另一个是其家族的人格。”春翠所获取的作品背后，同样流淌着“家族”与“私人”这两种意识的根基。当然，“家族”与“私人”并非能够被明确区分开来的，而是存在于“家族”之中的“私人”，或存在于“私人”之中的“家族”，正如淡水与咸水交融的汽水域一般，该收藏正是在“家族”与“私人”交织的独特价值观下逐步形成的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本展为纪念住友春翠逝世100周年，旨在介绍春翠所关注的近代美术。通过与生活在同一时代创作者们的交流，春翠究竟在注视着什么、追求着什么。本展将按时间顺序追溯春翠与作品之间的相遇（即美满的缘分），在重新审视其美学意识的同时，也将从收藏背景及时代性等视角出发，成为重新审视收藏形成史的一个契机。", "本展看点", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "1 与近代美术收藏代表作的再度重逢", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "春翠的品味常被赞誉为“典雅清淡”，确实，如今留存下来的众多作品都散发着格调高雅且清纯的意趣。本展将一次性公开汇聚于春翠身边的当时代美术，涵盖日本画、西洋画乃至工艺品，观众可通过这些作品一窥其美学意识的所在。此外，在当时由于向关联公司或个人的捐赠，春翠曾出手转让了自己收藏的部分作品。本展还将同时介绍住友旧藏的作品，对当时的收藏进行复原性的验证。", "translated": true}, "heading", "text": "2 以编年史展现的收藏轨迹", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本展将按时间顺序介绍春翠的生平与作品购买历史。作为一项全新尝试，会场墙面上将如年表般展示每年的大事件，并将其与相关事迹相联系，从而聚焦于收藏形成的各个方面。观众可以沿着春翠的足迹与收藏轨迹漫步前行、细细追溯。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/4-25.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "上岛凤山《十二个月美人》之“九月 菊花”明治42年（1909）泉屋博古馆东京 前期展出", "credit": "美術展ナビ", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "3 与同时代作家的交流", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "正如资助洋画家鹿子木孟郎赴巴黎留学的资金援助所代表的那样，春翠作为美术的庇护者，积极支援同时代的作家及美术团体。此外，通过春翠所喜好的茶道进行的交流，或亲自执笔、与心意相通的画家一同兴致勃勃地进行席画创作等，春翠打破了作家与赞助人之间的隔阂，与同时代的作家结下了亲密的交流。在展览中，不仅可以看到春翠购入的作品，还将介绍春翠与作家之间的逸闻趣事。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/5-23.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "板谷波山《葆光彩磁珍果文花瓶》重要文化财 大正6年（1917）泉屋博古馆东京", "credit": "美術展ナビ", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "展出结构", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "第1章 诺布勒斯·奥布利日（贵族的义务）的觉醒 明治25～36年，28～39岁", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "住友春翠（乳名·隆麿）于元治元年（1864）作为清华家之一的德大寺家第五子出生。在自幼学习汉籍与国书、爱好茶事·能乐·和歌的父亲公纯身边，他培养了身为公家（朝臣）的修养，并且还接受了德大寺家常客画师畑纲之赠予的绘画临摹范本等，在亲近美术的环境中长大成人。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "父亲去世后，他在学习院求学，后于明治25年作为住友家赘婿入赘，并于次年继承家督之位。春翠在致力于当时住友家所面临的重要课题的同时，于明治30年进行了为期约8个月的欧美视察，亲眼目实了欧美各国企业经营的实际状况以及实业家参与社会贡献的方式。回国后，他加深了对社会贡献的意识，并于明治36年作为第5届内国劝业博览会的协赞会会长及评议员，为博览会的成功倾注了全力。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在开展这些活动的同时，他也倾注全力于美术收藏，在日本画方面购入了田能村直入、村田香谷、桥本雅邦等当时重量级作家的作品，在西洋画方面接受其兄西园寺公望的建议，支援了黑田清輝与山本芳翠，并在欧美视察时购入了莫奈的作品。此外，以博览会为契机，他进一步推进了当代工艺品的收藏，这些藏品最终装饰了于明治36年竣工的须磨别邸。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/6-22.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "克劳德·莫奈《蒙索公园》1876年 泉屋博古馆东京 后期展出", "credit": "美術展ナビ", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "第2章 慈善事业的实践 明治37年～大正4年，40～51岁", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "于明治36年建设须磨别邸的春翠，随后着手建设了旨在取代延续了约280年之久的住友家本邸——鳗谷邸的新本邸。这座坐落于大阪茶臼山的宅邸凝聚了他特别的心血，春翠亲自前往建设现场并对细节下达指示，大正4年住宅部分基本建成，自宽永13年以来的本邸由此迁至此处。这座宅邸的营建也对春翠的美术收藏产生了影响，挑选出了适合装饰近代和风建筑的作品。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "另一方面，在欧美视察时深受芝加哥实业家马歇尔·菲尔德向美术馆捐款所打动的春翠，为大阪图书馆（现·大阪府立中之岛图书馆）捐赠了建设费及图书购置基金。不仅如此，他还构想设立大阪美术馆，着眼于向美术馆捐赠，在明治42年至大正3年期间集中购入了文展及巽画会等展览会的参展作品。这一时期的收藏，除了作为装饰宅邸的陈设这一侧面之外，其特征还在于旨在支援画家以及向社会进行文化回馈。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/3452d72557b50ef057bdcbc3c25c6867.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "安藤重兵卫《银七宝孔雀尾花瓶》明治36年（1903）泉屋博古馆东京", "credit": "美術展ナビ", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/8-18.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "迎田秋悦《秋草莳绘砚箱》大正时代·20世纪 泉屋博古馆东京 前期展出", "credit": "美術展ナビ", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/9-16.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "尾竹竹坡《九冠鸟》（右扇）明治45年（1912）泉屋博古馆东京", "credit": "美術展ナビ", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/10-15.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "香田胜太《春秋草花图》大正6～7年（1917～18）泉屋博古馆东京 前期展出", "credit": "美術展ナビ", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "第3章 贯穿“家族”与“私人”的事物 大正5年～大正15年，52～63岁", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "大正4年完成本邸搬迁的茶臼山邸，在此后继续推进了洋馆的扩建等工程，直到大正8年整体才终于竣工。然而仅仅两年之后，春翠便以建设美术馆为条件，将茶臼山的土地捐赠给了大阪市。这既是由于周边环境的变化，也是因为大阪市当时正在寻求美术馆用地的需求，而最重要的是，在大阪设立美术馆是春翠多年的夙愿。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在这一时期，通过展览会购入作品的情况逐渐减少，春翠与那些值得信赖的作家们加深了交流。特别是通过负责茶臼山邸所有门窗家具的表具师井口邨僊（井口古今堂第三代）的引荐，望月玉溪、上田耕甫等“古今堂网络”画家的作品开始被大量收藏。那些在床龛中显得潇洒典雅的画风完全符合春翠的美学意识，而且他们也是备受重用、能在贵宾面前即兴挥毫作画的画家。晚年的春翠在自己也喜爱书画的同时，与作家们建立了风雅之交，在通过这种交流所收集的作品中，浓重地体现了兼具“家族”与“私人”意识的春翠形象。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "为如今的住友集团奠定基础的住友家第15代当主·住友春翠。在他于明治至大正时期倾注热情的近代美术收藏背后，祈愿“家族”繁荣的意识与他本人对纯粹美之追求的“私人”意识交织出了绝妙的火花。本次为纪念逝世100周年的特展，不仅汇聚了藤岛武二、克劳德·莫奈、板谷波山等人的名作，还能以按时间顺序排列的编年史形式，细细追溯春翠与创作者们温暖交流的足迹。作为赞助人，亦作为一名美学爱好者，他究竟在凝视着什么、又将怎样的未来托付给了日本的近代美术，这无疑将是一次接触其独特美学意识的宝贵机会。（美术展ナビ） "作品が収蔵されるとき、その一つひとつにはそれぞれの物語があります。それは「いつ」「どこで」「誰が」「何を」「なぜ」「どのように」手に入れたのか―住友コレクションは、中国古代青銅器をはじめ、中国・日本書画、西洋絵画、近代陶磁器、茶道具、文房具、さらには能面・能装束など幅広い領域にわたりますが、その多くは、現在の住友グループの礎を築いた住友家第15代当主・住友吉左衞門 友純 （号：春翠、1864～1926）によって明治中頃から大正時代にかけて買い求められたものです。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "須磨別邸に訪れた洋画家・小杉 未醒 は、春翠の印象について「富豪は二重の人格を持つ、一つは富豪其人の人格、一は其の家の人格」と述べています。春翠が手に入れた作品にもまた、「家」と「私」というふたつの意識がその根底に流れています。もっとも、「家」と「私」は明確に区分できるものではなく、「家」のなかの「私」、あるいは「私」のなかの「家」があり、淡水と鹹水が混ざり合う汽水域のように、「家」と「私」とが交錯する独自の価値観のもと、このコレクションは形成されていきました。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本展は、住友春翠の没後100年を記念し、春翠が関心を寄せた近代美術を紹介するものです。同時代を生きた作り手たちとの交流を通じて、春翠が何をまなざし、何を求めたのか。本展では、春翠と作品とのめぐり合わせ（＝仕合せ）を時系列順に辿りながら、その美意識を見つめなおすとともに、収集の背景や時代性といった視点からコレクション形成史を再考する機会とします。"}, {"type": "image", article_text:
泉屋博古館（京都市）で、特別展「没後100年記念 住友春翠ー仕合せの住友近代美術コレクション」が10月31日から12月20日まで開催されます。

作品が収蔵されるとき、その一つひとつにはそれぞれの物語があります。それは「いつ」「どこで」「誰が」「何を」「なぜ」「どのように」手に入れたのか―住友コレクションは、中国古代青銅器をはじめ、中国・日本書画、西洋絵画、近代陶磁器、茶道具、文房具、さらには能面・能装束など幅広い領域にわたりますが、その多くは、現在の住友グループの礎を築いた住友家第15代当主・住友吉左衞門 友純 （号：春翠、1864～1926）によって明治中頃から大正時代にかけて買い求められたものです。

須磨別邸に訪れた洋画家・小杉 未醒 は、春翠の印象について「富豪は二重の人格を持つ、一つは富豪其人の人格、一は其の家の人格」と述べています。春翠が手に入れた作品にもまた、「家」と「私」というふたつの意識がその根底に流れています。もっとも、「家」と「私」は明確に区分できるものではなく、「家」のなかの「私」、あるいは「私」のなかの「家」があり、淡水と鹹水が混ざり合う汽水域のように、「家」と「私」とが交錯する独自の価値観のもと、このコレクションは形成されていきました。

本展は、住友春翠の没後100年を記念し、春翠が関心を寄せた近代美術を紹介するものです。同時代を生きた作り手たちとの交流を通じて、春翠が何をまなざし、何を求めたのか。本展では、春翠と作品とのめぐり合わせ（＝仕合せ）を時系列順に辿りながら、その美意識を見つめなおすとともに、収集の背景や時代性といった視点からコレクション形成史を再考する機会とします。

特別展 没後100年記念 住友春翠—仕合せの住友近代美術コレクション

会場：泉屋博古館（京都市左京区鹿ヶ谷下宮ノ前町24）

会期：2026年10月31日(土)〜12月20日(日) 前期：10月31日〜11月23日） 後期：11月25日〜12月20日 ＊会期中展示替えあり

開館時間：10:00〜17:00（最終入館時間 16:30）

休館日：月曜日、11月24日(火)（11月23日は開館）

観覧料：一般 1,200円、 学生 800円、18歳以下無料 ※障がい者手帳等を呈示のかたはご本人と同伴者1名まで無料 ※上記料金で併催のブロンズギャラリーもご覧になれます

詳細は、 泉屋博古館公式サイト まで。

本展のみどころ

1 近代美術コレクションの代表作と再会するコレクションたち

春翠の好みはしばしば「典雅清淡」と称されますが、確かに現在遺されている作品の数々は格調高く、そして清らかな趣をたたえています。本展では日本画や洋画、工芸まで、春翠のもとに集まった当代美術を一挙公開し、作品を通じてその美意識の在りかを見ることができます。また当時、関連会社や個人への寄贈により、春翠は自身が収蔵した作品の一部を手放しています。本展では、住友が旧蔵した作品を併せて紹介し、当時の収集について復原的に検証します。

2 クロニクルで魅せるコレクションの軌跡

本展では、春翠の経歴と作品購入の歴史が時系列順に紹介されます。新しい試みとして、会場の壁面には年表のように各年の出来事を掲示し、またその事蹟と紐づくかたちでコレクション形成の諸相に光が当てられます。春翠の足跡と収集の軌跡を歩きながらたどることができるでしょう。

3 同時代作家たちとの交流

洋画家・ 鹿子木孟郎 のパリ留学費用の資金援助に代表されるように、春翠は美術の庇護者として積極的に同時代の作家や美術団体を支援しました。また春翠が嗜んだ茶の湯を通じた交流、あるいは自ら筆を執り、気心の知れた画家とともに席画に興じるなど、春翠は作家とパトロンの垣根を超え、同時代の作家と親しく交流を結んでいます。展覧会では、春翠が買い求めた作品を見ることができるとともに春翠と作家のエピソードが紹介されます。

展示構成

第1章 ノブレス・オブリージュの目覚め 明治25～36年、28～39歳

住友春翠（幼名・隆麿）は、元治元年（1864）、 清華家 の徳大寺家の第五子として生まれました。幼少より漢籍や国書を学び、茶事・能楽・詠歌を嗜む父 公純 のもとで公家としての教養を身につけ、また徳大寺家出入りの絵師・ 畑綱之 から絵手本を与えられるなど、美術にも親んで育ちました。

父の死後、学習院で学んだのち、明治25年に住友家に婿養子として入家、翌年に家督を相続しています。春翠は当時住友家が抱えていた重要課題に取り組む一方、明治30年には約8か月に及ぶ欧米視察を行い、欧米諸国における企業経営の実態や実業家による社会貢献の在り方を目撃しています。帰国後は社会貢献への意識を深め、明治36年には第5回内国勧業博覧会の協賛会会長・評議員として博覧会の成功に尽力しています。

こうした活動と並行して美術収集にも力を注ぎ、日本画では 田能村直入 、村田香谷、橋本雅邦といった当時の重鎮作家らの作品を購入し、洋画では兄・西園寺公望の助言を受けて黒田清輝や山本芳翠を支援したほか、欧米視察の際にはモネの作品を購入しました。また博覧会を契機に当代工芸品の収集も進め、これらは明治36年に竣工した須磨別邸を飾ることになりました。

第2章 フィランソロピーの実践 明治37年～大正4年、40～51歳

明治36年に須磨別邸を建設した春翠は、続いて約280年にわたり住友家の本邸であった鰻谷邸に代わる新たな本邸の建設に着手しました。大阪・茶臼山に築かれたこの邸宅は、春翠自らが建設現場に足を運び細部まで指示を与えるなど特別な意を注いだもので、大正4年に住宅部分がほぼ完成し、寛永13年以来の本邸がここへ移されました。この築邸は春翠の美術収集にも影響を与え、近代和風建築を飾るにふさわしい作品が選ばれていきました。

一方、欧米視察の際にシカゴの実業家マーシャル・フィールドの美術館寄付に感銘を受けた春翠は、大阪図書館（現・大阪府立中之島図書館）の建設費や図書購入基金を寄付しています。さらに大阪美術館の設置を構想し、美術館への寄贈を見据えて、明治42年から大正3年にかけて文展や 巽画会 などの展覧会出品作を集中的に購入しています。この時期の収集は、邸宅を飾る調度としての側面に加え、画家の支援や社会への文化的還元を志向した点に特徴があります。

第3章 「家」と「私」を貫くもの 大正5年～大正15年、52～63歳

大正4年に本邸の移転を終えた茶臼山邸は、その後も洋館の増築などが進められ、大正8年にようやく全体が完成しました。しかしそのわずか2年後、春翠は美術館建設を条件に茶臼山の敷地を大阪市へ寄付することになります。周辺環境の変化に加え、大阪市が美術館用地を求めていた事情によるものであり、なによりも大阪に美術館を設けることは春翠の長年の願いでした。

この時期には展覧会での作品購入が次第に減少していき、春翠は信頼する作家たちとの交流を深めています。とくに茶臼山邸の建具一切を手がけた表具師・井口 邨僊 （井口 古今堂 三代目）の取り次ぎにより、望月 玉渓 や上田 耕甫 ら「古今堂ネットワーク」の画家の作品が多く収集されるようになります。床の間に映える瀟洒で典雅な作風は、春翠の美意識にかなうものであり、また彼らは賓客の前で即興の席画を揮うなど重用された画家でした。晩年の春翠は自らも書画を嗜みながら作家と文雅の交わりを結び、その交流のなかで集められた作品には、「家」と「私」の意識をあわせ持つ春翠の姿が色濃く表れています。

現在の住友グループの礎を築いた住友家第15代当主・住友春翠。彼が明治から大正にかけて情熱を注いだ近代美術収集の背景には、「家」の繁栄を願う意識と、彼自身の純粋な美への探求心である「私」の意識が絶妙に交錯していました。今回の没後100年を記念した特別展では、藤島武二やクロード・モネ、板谷波山らの名作が一堂に会するだけでなく、春翠と作り手たちとの温かな交流の足跡を時系列のクロニクル形式でじっくりと辿ることができます。パトロンとして、また一人の美の愛好家として彼が何を見つめ、日本の近代美術にどのような未来を託したのか、その独自の美意識に触れる貴重な機会となりそうです。（美術展ナビ） ◇東京会場レポート

title_original: Matthew Connors confronts a challenging modern world in The Axe Will Survive the Master
editorial_title_zh: 马修·康纳斯（Matthew Connors）在新书《斧头将留存主人》（The Axe Will Survive the Master）中直面充满挑战的现代世界
editorial_excerpt_zh: 马修·康纳斯通过其摄影集《斧头将留存主人》（The Axe Will Survive the Master），为现代世界的冲突与威权主义提供了引人入胜的洞察
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "作为三部曲摄影集中的第三部，马修·康纳斯（Matthew Connors）汇集了历时12年创作的影像，其最新作品向一个充斥着暴力与不确定性的世界提出了严峻的问题", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“斧头总是在那里，随时待命。主人的斧头……能挺过一切。永远不要忘记这一点。”这些话出自苏联秘密警察内务人民委员部（NKVD）的一名前行刑者之口，被斯维特拉娜·阿列克谢耶维奇（Svetlana Alexievich）记录在其关于苏联解体的大型口述历史著作《二手时间》（Secondhand Time: The Last of the Soviets）中。马修·康纳斯（Matthew Connors）唤起这种情感，是为了完成一项更为雄心勃勃的事业：对我们当代世界进行摄影式的洞察。这些影像历时12年在曼谷、开罗、切尔诺贝利、香港、基辅、那不勒斯、平壤、瓦拉纳西和华盛顿特区等城市拍摄。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这里存在一种危险，即如此宏大散乱的主题可能会消散于无形——如果一件事物讲的是一切，那它是否什么也没讲？——但康纳斯将叙事控制得很紧凑。开篇几页聚焦于公共空间中的平坦平面、广告和图像，随后叙事扩展至暴力与镇压的场景。该书分为多个章节，例如“有瑕疵的起源”（maculate是immaculate的反义词）或“阴谋的核心”。人们往往很难判断康纳斯是在哪里拍摄的特定镜头，这表明这些不同的地点有着许多共同点：全球化已经拉平了不同文化之间的差异，相同的服饰、科技和不断抬头的威权主义映射到了每一个地方。", "translated": true}, {"type": "quote", "text": "人们往往很难判断康纳斯是在哪里拍摄的特定镜头，这表明这些不同的地点有着许多共同点", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本书的封面引人入胜，描绘了一块碎成圆形的玻璃，这也让人联想到相机镜头；这里或许存在一种元批评，即相机本身就是问题的一部分。照片展示了一个由于图像、巨幅广告牌以及与平坦平面和局部视野相交织的倒影而部分破碎的现实；与此同时，激光笔和面具记录了逃避监控的尝试。康纳斯撰写的文本《打结的同盟》（The Knotted Alliance）采用第一人称复数（“我们”）写成，描述了一份由多人批注和更新的请愿书；它指向了一种集体努力。围绕着集体与个人、达成共识的能力，或者——如阿列克谢耶维奇那样——汇聚众多声音，发生了一些有趣的事情。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "康纳斯的作品融入其中处于何种位置尚无定论。他的场景组合是否暗示了一种多声部的感觉？还是体现了他对事物的独特视角的组织性视野？相机是否允许我们思考个人的视角，或者——正如唐娜·哈拉维（Donna Haraway）所说——鼓励了一种“上帝视角”（“god trick”），即一切似乎都从虚无中被看到？结论并不容易得出，但这本书提出了重大的问题，并为它们的紧迫性进行了辩护。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "马修·Connors的《斧头将留存主人》（The Axe Will Survive the Master）由 SPBH Editions/MACK 出版，定价£50。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "mackbooks.co.uk", "links": [{"text": "mackbooks.co.uk", "url": "https://mackbooks.co.uk/"}], "translated": true}]

article_text:
The third in a trilogy of photobooks, collating images made over 12 years, Matthew Connors’ latest work asks demanding questions of a world facing violence and uncertainty

“The axe is always there, ready. The master’s axe… survives everything. Don’t ever forget it.” These words were spoken by a former executioner for the NKVD (the Soviet secret police) and recorded by Svetlana Alexievich in Secondhand Time: The Last of the Soviets , her epic oral history on the collapse of the USSR. Matthew Connors evokes the sentiment for something even more ambitious; a photographic insight into our contemporary world, made over 12 years in cities such as Bangkok, Cairo, Chernobyl, Hong Kong, Kyiv, Naples, Pyongyang, Varanasi and Washington DC.

There is a danger that such a sprawling topic can dissipate into nothing – if something is about everything is it about anything? – but Connors keeps the narrative tight. The opening pages focus on flat planes and ads and images in public space, the narrative then expands out to scenes of violence and repression. The book is divided into chapters such as ‘Maculate Origins’ (maculate is the opposite of immaculate) or ‘A Caucus of Shadows’. It is often hard to judge where Connors has taken particular shots, suggesting that the many locations have much in common; globalisation has flattened differences between cultures, the same clothes, technology and rising authoritarianism mapping onto everywhere.

It is often hard to judge where Connors has taken particular shots, suggesting that the many locations have much in common

The book cover is intriguing, depicting glass smashed into a circle that also suggests a camera lens; there is maybe a metacriticism at work here, in which the camera is part of the problem. The photographs show a reality fracturing partly because of images, billboards and reflections intersecting with flat planes and fragments of views; meanwhile laser pointers and masks document attempts to evade surveillance. Connors’ text, The Knotted Alliance , is written in first-person plural (‘we’) and describes a petition annotated and updated by many hands; it refers to a group effort. There is something interesting going on around the group versus the individual, the ability to reach a consensus, or – as in Alexievich’s case – to gather many voices.

Where Connors’ images fit into that is moot. Does his assemblage of scenes suggest a sense of the polyvocal? Or the organising perspective of his particular vision of things? Does the camera allow us to think of the individual point of view or – as Donna Haraway had it – encourage a “god trick” in which everything is apparently seen from nowhere? Conclusions are not easy to draw, but this book is asking the big questions, and making a case for their urgency.

The Axe Will Survive the Master by Matthew Connors is published by SPBH Editions/MACK, priced £50.

article_text:
When Sotheby’s reported first-half consolidated sales of $4.4 billion in July , some suggested that the business was now stretching beyond the auction room and into hospitality and real estate. If this Frieze Week is anything to go by, it seems smaller art fairs like Minor Attractions and London Invitational (an extension of the Dallas Invitational) have also taken note.

Minor Attractions changed locations for its fourth edition and picked The Newman as its new home, a recently opened hotel in central London. And for the London Invitational’s inaugural fair, running through Sunday, 13 suites at The Chancery Rosewood in Mayfair have been taken over by galleries including Andrew Reed Gallery, Broadway, Charles Asprey, Europa, François Ghebaly, James Cope Gallery, James Kelly Contemporary, Lomex, Marinaro, Franklin Parrasch Gallery and Vardaxoglou. The all-suite property ranges from £1,200 to £24,000 ($1,600 to $32,000) per night and opened its doors back in September.

James Cope, the British-born, Dallas-based art dealer and founder of the fair, told ARTnews this model is slowing down the art fair experience. It’s what’s needed, he said, when the market is “slow and steady” after the sudden splurge post-Covid.

“I hate hearing about the doom and gloom of the art market—it’s not in a bad place. We’re just coming out of a real bullish market and everyone’s recalibrating,” he added.

Cope, who participated in Frieze London with his namesake gallery, is intentionally alluding to a bygone era of art fairs with his participation in the Dallas and London Invitationals. (New York’s Armory Show began in 1994 in the small rooms of the Gramercy Park Hotel in New York.) “This environment creates a more human time with dealers, collectors, curators and being in a domestic setting helps you understand how the artwork might look in your home,” Cope said.

He said his measure of success extends beyond the transactions taking place—even though the participating galleries in the Dallas Invitational have continuously returned, which shows “business is being done.”

“Are people happy and smiling? I’m a gallery owner, and I want to obviously make sales and enjoy my time,” Cope said.

In his suite, he had the works of young artists Michelle Rawlings and Coco Young on display, fitting right into the plush wooden interiors of the hotel. Cope’s collector demographic runs from mid- to late 20s and 30s to established collectors in their 50s, 60s and 70s who work in industries such as shipping, oil, gas and banking.

The London Invitational may be intimate, but the sums associated with its offerings are big.

The Los Angeles–based gallery Bel Ami offered pieces from several of its artists: Minami Kobayashi, Guillaume Dénervaud, Soshiro Matsubara, Isabelle Frances McGuire, Dan Mitchell, Ian Miyamura, Lauren Satlowski, and Marina Stern, ranging from $5,000 to $33,000. Matsubara’s work is currently on display at the Gagosian London as part of the René Magritte exhibition “This Is Still Not a Pipe: The Afterlife of Magritte,” which has been the gallery’s most visited show to date in London.

Bel Ami director Lee Foley told ARTnews that she has found avid interest in her artists from new collectors ages between 20 and 40 that work in film and tech. “There is something special about the art scene being a close-knit community in a time when that’s harder and harder to find. It’s our job to teach new collectors about the artists as we rely on them for business,” Foley said.

At Franklin Parrasch Gallery, the works start from £2,800 ($3,700) and go into the high five figures; they range from Peter Alexander’s block wedges to Soyoung Lee’s distorted portraits to Sylvia Snowden’s abstract figures to Joe Goode’s blue skies. Franklin Parrasch, the gallery’s namesake founder, told ARTnews that he joined the London Invitational because he’s interested in new ways to “shape the model,” and the current trend is to include experiences with understanding art to counteract a “struggling market.”

“At the same time, I think artists are finding ways to survive and thrive in their own environments. Sometimes not having the copious amounts of money they were making a few years back is good for generating new energy and thought in other areas besides commerce,” Parrasch said, noting that collectors are less impulsive in their purchases.

Responding to the tough market, New York dealer Lauren Marinaro of Marinaro Gallery took a conscious decision to feature artworks under $10,000 from artists Ever Baldwin, Ridley Howard, Ron Isaacs, Ryan Johnson and Alessandro Teoldi.

“It’s an approachable number right now and a way for introducing my program to London,” she told ARTnews . “It’s definitely been a hard three to four years, but there’s been a light at the end of the tunnel in the past six months. Art advisers are doing really good work in educating people that’s resulted in new collectors coming in and meeting a lot of young people.”

The London Invitational also gave two dealers without galleries the opportunity to exhibit their artists.

Dealer Charles Asprey displayed Alessandro Raho’s small to large paintings ranging from £6,000 to £35,000 ($8,000 to $46,8000) depicting scenes from Los Angeles to the flowers found in his London home. The artist’s most famous work is a portrait of actor Judi Dench at the National Portrait Gallery in London.

“My artist doesn’t like exhibiting on white walls and the art world has changed, you don’t necessarily need physical spaces anymore to represent someone,” said Asprey, who is also a trustee at Institute of Contemporary Arts in London.

At Frieze London and the London Invitational, the London-versus-Paris debate remained a topic of conversation. The New York–based gallery Broadway tested out the waters by doing both fairs; the gallery participated in Frieze London two years ago.

“We felt that the combination of these fairs despite what’s been going on with the popularity of Art Basel Paris is that London is getting its footing back,” Joe Cole, cofounder of Broadway, told ARTnews , adding that the gallery had its strongest curatorial attendance at Frieze London on the VIP day. “I certainly met a number of new collectors from the UK, Europe, and the Middle East that I don’t think I would have met in the US.”

Now that London Invitational has extended to the UK, is Paris next on the cards? “I don’t really like Paris,” Cope said, praising London for its metropolitan nature. “There’s people from Asia and the Middle East and Russia and everywhere in London. There’s so much hype around Paris and I’m not trying to compete with that.”
excerpt_original: The London-versus-Paris debate poured over to the intimate fair at The Chancery Rosewood in Mayfair.

editorial_title_zh: 何为家园？：2026年Menart艺术博览会
editorial_excerpt_zh: Menart艺术博览会于10月23-25日举行，该展会专门致力于展示代理来自...
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "在巴黎，Menart艺术博览会在繁华的艺术周与动荡的城市背景下，审视着“家园”的意义。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Menart艺术博览会迎来第七届，于10月23–25日举办。展会专为代理中东和北非（MENA）地区艺术家的画廊而设，核心围绕一个存在主义的疑问：“家园在何方？”归属感、领土、流亡、侨民、归途：这一概念在遗产与未来之间摇摆，也在世间生存那不断变化的身份状态之间摇摆。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Menart艺术博览会创始人兼总监劳拉·德·欧特维尔（Laure d’Hauteville）是一位专注于中东和北非地区的艺术顾问兼策展人。1998年，她创立了贝鲁特首个现当代艺术博览会（一直持续到2005年），随后又创办了贝鲁特艺术博览会（2010–19年）。她在2021年推出了Menart艺术博览会。“创立它的初衷是为来自中东和北非的艺术家在欧洲提供一个真正的可见度平台——不是通过改造他们来迎合西方视角，而是让他们以原本的身份、他们的出处以及他们实践赖以发展的语境被看见和理解，”她解释道。“只要有可能，我都希望画廊直接来自贝鲁特、大马士革、突尼斯、阿尔及尔、迪拜、阿布扎比、利雅得、德黑兰或该地区的其他地方。我希望艺术家们带着自己的声音、自己的参考坐标、自己的历史来到巴黎，而不是首先经过欧洲视角的过滤。这种真实性对我来说极其重要。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "德·欧特维尔对当前的挑战有着清醒的认识。“那些来自经历极端艰难环境的国家的画廊和艺术家们的出席，令我动容，”她说道。“例如，当一家画廊今天从大马士革来到巴黎，这种出场本身就超越了参加一场艺术博览会的意义。它在诉说：我们在这里，我们仍在创作，我们有话要对世界说。”", "translated": "本届展会汇集了来自18个国家的34家画廊，展出了上百位艺术家（58位男性和47位女性）。它在巴黎艺术周期间举办，这是国际艺术市场上的一个决定性时刻，能在收藏家为这座城市丰富的艺术活动而齐聚一堂之际带来本土可见度。然而，今年却是一个微妙的时刻，法国激荡的抗议活动营造了一个紧张的背景：巴黎巴塞尔艺术展（Art Basel Paris）和一些巴黎本地画廊为了防范周末可能出现的骚乱而提前闭馆。", article_text:
In Paris, Menart Fair interrogates the meaning of home against a busy art week and turbulent city.

Running from October 23–25, Menart Fair – exclusively dedicated to galleries representing artists from the MENA region – returns for its 7th edition, centred on the existential query: “Where is home?” Belonging, territory, exile, diaspora, a point of return: the concept oscillates between heritage and future, between the shifting status of existing in the world.

Founder/director of Menart Fair, Laure d’Hauteville is an art consultant and curator specialising in the MENA region. In 1998, she founded Beirut’s first modern and contemporary art fair, which ran until 2005, and subsequently created the Beirut Art Fair (2010–19). She developed Menart Fair in 2021. “It was created to give artists from the Middle East and North Africa a genuine platform for visibility in Europe – not by transforming them to fit a Western perspective, but by allowing them to be seen and understood for who they are, where they come from, and within the contexts in which their practices have developed,” she explains. “Whenever possible, I want the galleries to come directly from Beirut, Damascus, Tunis, Algiers, Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Riyadh, Tehran or elsewhere in the region. I want the artists to arrive in Paris with their own voices, their own references, their own histories, without having first been filtered through a European reading. That authenticity is extremely important to me.”

D’Hauteville is well aware of current challenges. “I am moved by the presence of galleries and artists coming from countries experiencing extremely difficult circumstances,” she says. “When a gallery comes from Damascus to Paris today, for example, this presence means something beyond participation in an art fair. It says we are here, we continue to create and we have something to say to the world.”

She refuses also to put forth a reductive depiction. “In a region experiencing wars, conflicts, economic crises, displacement and profound social transformations, continuing to create, exhibit, travel, exchange and bring artists together is already a powerful act.”

The fair brings together 34 galleries from 18 countries, showcasing more than a hundred artists (58 men and 47 women). It takes place during Paris Art Week, a decisive moment within the international art market, enabling local visibility while collectors are in town for the city’s extensive art offer. This year was an odd moment, however, as the protests roiling France created a fraught backdrop: Art Basel Paris and some Paris-based galleries were closing early in anticipation of unrest over the weekend.

Held on two levels at a space in the Marais, on the downstairs floor, visitors encountered Shiva Zahed Gallery, opened in Istanbul in February, where the eponymous Iranian founder showcases artists from her native country. Here, there are perforated geometric art works by Reza Lavassani from the series Khayyam , in which Islamic iconography is hand-done on rectangles of cardboard (and even on a flattened pizza box). Zahed notes that, though framed here, the works are extra beautiful when backlit and light shines through the tiny holes. Nearby, Zahed is showing Mahsa Karimizadeh, whose cropped pencil drawings from 2024 spotlight a tense torso – the artist was dealing with cancer – which function as studies for black-painted foam sculptures from 2025 featuring the folds of her body. Nearby, at Galerie Bessieres Art Contemporain, Lebanese photographer Serge Najjar’s stunning images are inspired by Russian Constructivism (His Instagram bio tellingly states “It is not about what you see but how you see it.”) He turns angled architecture into a stark geometric backdrop with shapely windows and high-contrast shadows. His work will be part of a show at the Institut du Monde Arabe in Paris next March.

Just behind this booth, at Kalim Bechara Art Gallery from Lebanon, Lebanese artist – and associate at Christie’s – Mira El Khalil shows a startling oil on canvas work, Holiday Inn Beirut from 2026. The huge building is seen sinking amid the sea, the blue-green waters lapping against the submerging grid of dark windows. This painting was accompanied by two others, of a portrait and a couple.

Upstairs, under a luminous skylight, Negah Art Gallery from Tehran is showing Iran-born NYC-based illustrator Farshid Shafiey’s joyful Head over Heels series of shimmying bodies in vibrant colours. Further in, at MS Art Gallery from Beirut, Tony Mhanna – a mechanical engineer by trade – has dramatically photographed swathes of fabrics floating in grand abandoned staircases in Beirut, in his series WRAITH . These photos shared wall space with colourful graphic rugs from Hala Salem.

The Project Room, curated by Wassyla Tamzali, features 12 artists living and working in Algeria. In her introductory text, Tamzali cited Etel Adnan on beauty as “that fusion of talent and thought”. Amongst the dozen artists, Mounir Gouri’s poetic Routes cousues (2017), includes four framed groupings of four ceramic plates, each with tiny holes connected by black thread like constellations.

Despite the turmoil, in Paris itself and in the world at large, the fair is a place that holds space for creativity. As d’Hauteville asserts, “The MENA region should not only reach European audiences through the vocabulary of crisis, war or geopolitics. It is also a region of immense creativity, humour, beauty, intellectual energy, youth and imagination.”

Menart Fair runs until 25 October

*Menart closed on Saturday 24 October due to protests across France, in alignment with other fairs including Art Basel Paris

article_text:
There is a famous skit in Spike Jonze’s 2003 skate video, Yeah Right! , featuring Owen Wilson in the middle of his run as Hollywood’s golden boy. Sitting in an open hatchback wearing a black jacket and a “Girl” hat—a nod to Jonze’s skateboard company—Wilson playfully nags skaters Mike Carroll, Rick Howard, and Eric Koston about the tricks they performed earlier in the video. Ty Evans’s camera—outfitted with a fish-eye lens whose capacity to capture wide angles adds a warped intimacy to the scene—bounces between the characters, as Carroll puts Wilson on the spot about his tricks. The actor begins listing his many skating feats: “Hollywood High, what did I do? . . . Don’t forget Sylmar! Front salad, back salad, front blunt. Basically, I’ve got two minutes of footy.” He gets up (“Carroll, will you crack my back?”), sheds his jacket, and yells “No warm-up! First try, bitch!” as he drops the board and starts pushing. He approaches a rail, leaps up, and hits a bluntside. Wilson fist bumps the cameraman: “Yeah right!”

On the level of form, this interlude has a practical effect: it injects levity into an otherwise intense hour-long athletic spectacle. But Jonze also uses the skit to disorient the viewer, inviting them to question what they just saw. Was Wilson’s inventory of trick names scripted? Did the actor actually slide down the pole and (somewhat) stomp the trick? (The sketchy landing only adds an element of realism to the otherwise surreal occurrence.) Maybe he is actually… good at skating? Only the most hawk-eyed viewer would notice that, during a quick camera pivot, Wilson is replaced by a stunt double: Koston in a blond wig.

Yeah Right! represents the best of the skate video, a form that has never really gotten its critical due in its 60-year existence. Jonze’s classic arrived at the height of what many skaters describe as the Golden Age of skate videos, which included gems such as Alien Workshop’s Photosynthesis (2000) and Mind Field (2009); Emerica’s This is Skateboarding (2003), The DC Video (2003), and Baker 3 (2005), and Vicious Cycle (2005); and Lakai’s Fully Flared (2007). Jonze, who became a critical darling with Being John Malkovich in 1999, had come into his own as a filmmaker through the world of skateboarding: he made Rubbish Heap for World Industries in 1989, Video Days for Blind Skateboards in 1991, and the surreal cult classic Mouse for Girl Skateboards in 1996. Yeah Right! was different: it was technically rigorous, though still spiritually DIY. It was committed to the traditions of skate video aesthetics—the handheld feel (popularized by skating’s most famous camera , the Sony VX1000), the grittiness, the underground vibe—but resistant to formulas. Most of all, it presented skaters doing real tricks in ways that were formally imaginative: in the opening scene, Jonze used ultra slow motion, a first for skate videos at the time, and later, in the “invisible board” skit, he created the illusion that skaters were riding on air.

Right from its very beginnings, the beauty and tension of the skate film came from the ground up. Noel Black’s boy-meets-girl short Skaterdater (1965), the first film ever made about skating, turned Southern California’s pristine suburban life upside down with two choices: placing the camera at ankle-level to shoot the skaters, and showing them riding on their bare feet, skidding and moving about on the asphalt. The cleanliness of the skaters’ “prep” attire contrasts with the filth they accumulate with each kick. The film, which was nominated for Best Short Subject (Live Action) at the 1966 Academy Awards and won both the Best Short Film Grand Prix and Technical Grand Prize at the 1966 Cannes Film Festival, brought viewers down to the street level. A camera was affixed to an outrigger platform connected to a bicycle, viscerally communicating the feeling of freedom and risk afforded by a skateboard.

Skaterdater ’s crafty use of camera angles has influenced the way in which skating is understood in the broader culture. In the 1970s, the Z-Boys, a group of teen surfers-turned-skaters from Dogtown, in Southern California, became associated with a hardcore aesthetic that matched the grit of the stretch between Venice Beach and the Santa Monica Pier. In photos, many of which were taken by Craig Stecyk , the kids look badass with their exaggerated leans and boisterous personalities. Stecyk often positioned himself downhill, looking up at the Z-Boys carving toward him. In a now-iconic 1975 shot, Stecyk captures Jay Adams yoking his board around a cone in a deep squat on Bicknell Hill in Santa Monica, his hand scraping the ground like a motorcycle racer’s knee on a curve. In another photo, Stecyk positions himself on the side of an empty pool as Adams, holding his board with one hand and tapping his back trucks along the pool’s edge, looks directly into the camera, giving it the finger.

In 1984, Stacy Peralta, the standout skater from that group, directed and co-produced The Bones Brigade Video Show , which featured legends like Lance Mountain, Tony Hawk, Steve Caballero, and Rodney Mullen. Whereas the Z-Boys look like punk superstars in Stecyk’s photos, the Video Show told a different skate story: it presented the sport as an everyman’s pursuit. Mountain leisurely skates around Los Angeles, often on sidewalks, occasionally planting on walls, kicking and pushing on his board without a lot of technically over-the-top maneuvers. He is just coasting, and the camera observes him with equal chill, often from stationary positions and straight-ahead, eye-level angles.

The Bones Brigade was a team representing Powell-Peralta, a skateboard company started by Peralta and George Powell (with Stecyk as creative director), so pandering to a more general audience made business sense. Powell-Peralta’s later efforts— Future Primitive (1985), The Search for Animal Chin (1987), and Ban This (1989), among others—continued to promote skating as a lifestyle, and they also offered, through fly-on-the-wall depictions of the skaters’ rituals, rites, and kinship, a window into a seemingly closed subculture. The Bones Brigade, for instance, were shown traveling together, pushing each other to experiment, and expressing awe at one another’s trick arsenal.

The idea of community is paramount in the most well-known documentaries about skating: Dogtown and Z-Boys (2001); Bones Brigade: An Autobiography (2012); and All the Streets Are Silent: The Convergence of Hip Hop and Skateboarding 1987-1997 (2021). In narrative films like Larry Clark’s Kids (1995) and Jonah Hill’s mid90s (2018), skating is a refuge for misfits and punks trying to make connections outside of broken homes. But the communal third spaces—skate and surf shops—where these young (almost always) men congregated also reinforce the ways in which late-capitalist notions of identity defined skate culture. The history of skate videos is also a history of advertising investments made by skate brands. Empire Skate , a documentary that aired last year as part of ESPN’s 30 for 30 series, shows how the kids who created New York street skating culture also helped Supreme appropriate it into a global commodity. The brand engineered its image using real skaters, who lent it street cred. In return, Supreme provided resources—a hangout spot, clothes, jobs.

These videos were commercials that resembled high art. Thomas Campbell’s A Love Supreme , a promo video he filmed for the Supreme store in 1995, is shot in black and white, with John Coltrane’s classic album A Love Supreme as the soundtrack. The film is less concerned with skating as an athletic endeavor and more interested in its setting—in this case, New York City. Campbell interweaves shots of skaters moving in and out of traffic with shots of businessmen walking through revolving doors, silhouettes of people kissing, pedestrian overpass stairs, panhandlers, shoes being lobbed over light poles, pay phones, the subway, park foliage, out-of-focus headlights. The video contributes to the lore of Supreme’s origin story, as recounted in Empire Skate and All the Streets Are Silent , which was about aligning skating and visual art—the brand’s logo appropriates the aesthetic of Barbara Kruger, and the shop was designed to look like an art gallery.

Skate culture has been shaped not only by brand endorsements and cool tricks, but also by the consistent criminalization of the sport. In the ’70s, at the height of the Southern California drought, the Z-Boys would trespass into private backyards to skate in dry, unused pools. In the ’90s, street skaters found exciting alternative uses and misuses of city infrastructure, repurposing loading docks, freeway offramps, benches, and concrete walls as makeshift skate parks. These creative uses of public and private infrastructure made them the frequent targets of police violence and harassment. The need to evade the wrath of cops and property owners helped refine skate video aesthetics. If you need to film someone getting a trick off in a spot where you’re not supposed to be, you need to film everything, get in and out quickly, and evaluate what you have after the fact. That’s one reason why, historically, so many skate videos have a verité sensibility.

Music lends a richness of texture to the onscreen tricks as well. Freestyles from the likes of Method Man, Ghostface Killah, Busta Rhymes, and Fat Joe (lifted from radio’s The Stretch Armstrong and Bobbito Show ) add rawness to footage of skaters like Harold Hunter and Danny Supa ripping in the streets of New York in Zoo York – Mixtape (1998). It’s one thing to see Zered Bassett in Vicious Cycle ride up the wall of an office building but another to see it with Jay-Z rapping “When the streets is watching/Blocks keep clocking/Waiting for you to break, make your first mistake/Can’t ignore it” on the soundtrack. A killer score is not just about song choice, it’s also about timing: a perfectly synced chord change hitting just as a skater stomps a landing or eats shit, mixing with the sounds of skating itself—the cling and drag of metal trucks hitting a rail, the rhythmic growl of wheels picking up speed on a sidewalk, the pop of the wood when a skater pushes off the ground on an ollie (or nollie), the eruption of cheers after someone narrowly avoids catastrophe.

One of my favorite moments from a skate film comes from Jeff Stevens’s segment in the first A Happy Medium (2008) by Buster O’Shea. Stevens seems bent on touching every bannister, every support beam, every curb with his board. He booger slides. He primo slides, grinding on a loading dock only to half-flip his board on its edge and coast a little more, standing on the sides of his wheels before jumping 180 out of it. The video is shot in Phoenix, Arizona. Many of the shots are at night—it’s too hot during the day to skate. This brings the presence of the cameraman into the shots via shadows more than we’re used to in most tapes. Happy Medium depicts what I might call drought-resistant skating—in lieu of city benches and construction ramps, the skaters leap over cactuses and succulents, roll over poorly-landscaped front yards, and skid down barren aqueducts. The landscape is completely washed out.

It’s a tall order for art to approach lived experience. But, since Skaterdater , that’s exactly what all skate videos try to do in one way or another. The Golden Age might be over, but in the last few decades, other skate videos—Girl/Chocolate’s Pretty Sweet (2012), Supreme’s “ cherry” (2014), HUF’s Forever (2023), Dickies’s Honeymoon (2024)—have kept this spirit alive. They speak to something essential about the form: that the best videos help you see skating like a skater. They offer another way of looking.

article_text:
Connor Storrie is circling a role opposite Ryan Gosling in Marvel Studios ‘ Ghost Rider , sources have confirmed to Deadline.

Reps for Marvel declined to comment. There’s word yet on the role to be played by Storrie, though he’s reportedly the film’s villain. Reuniting Gosling with his Star Wars: Starfighter director Shawn Levy and that film’s writer, Jonathan Tropper, the comic book movie is slated for release on July 28, 2028. Marvel dropped the bombshell of its announcement at this year’s San Diego Comic-Con, with production slated for 2027.

Ghost Rider is the alter ego of Johnny Blaze, a stunt motorcyclist who, in Marvel comics, makes a deal with the demon Mephisto to save his adoptive father and becomes bound to the Spirit of Vengeance. Created by writer Gary Friedrich, artist Mike Ploog, and Roy Thomas — Stan Lee’s first successor as editor-in-chief of Marvel Comics — he first appeared in Marvel Spotlight #5 in 1972. Nicolas Cage famously brought the character to screens in a pair of earlier Marvel films, 2007’s Ghost Rider and 2011’s Ghost Rider: Spirit of Vengeance .

Related Stories

Amanda Seyfried Explains Turning Down 'Guardians Of The Galaxy' For Family: "Just Not For Me"

'Avengers: Doomsday' World Series Sneak Peek Sees Mister Fantastic Throw Out First Pitch

Storrie has broken out as one of the buzziest names of the moment with Heated Rivalry , Crave/HBO Max’s queer hockey romance based on the Game Changers book series by Rachel Reid, where he stars opposite Hudson Williams. The show is presently heading into its second season.

Watch on Deadline

Since the show’s November 2025 debut, Storrie has had his pick of projects. Others upcoming for him include Craig Zobel’s thriller Turpentine opposite Melissa McCarthy, A24’s Please from Halina Reijn and Peaked from Molly Gordon, and Sarah Polley’s The Bell Jar for Focus Features. Notably, following his Heated Rivalry breakout, he also earned an Emmy nomination for a hosting appearance on Saturday Night Live .

THR was first to the news of the actor’s big new gig.

"paragraph", "text": "在马达玛宫（Palazzo Madama），“城市之躯：1884.1961年新艺术与现代之间的时尚与艺术”（Il corpo della città. Moda e arti tra Liberty o modernità 1884.1961）正在展出，它提供了一个独特的视角来观察都灵这座城市通过身体的发展演变，身体不仅被视为艺术主体，更被用作反映社会、经济和文化变迁的空间，是时尚、艺术与城市转型之间交汇的理想场所。展览动线引领参观者走过一条由19至20世纪各大博览会串联起来的路线。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "由克莉莉·阿尔纳迪·迪·巴尔梅（Clelia Arnaldi di Balme）策展的展览“花园：18世纪体验自然之美”（Giardini. Enigma contemporaneo），呈现了一位在该家族收藏史与画廊展览规划中居于核心地位的艺术家。德·基里科的作品与精选的历史及当代艺术家作品展开对话，这些艺术家以不同方式承袭了他的遗产，通过自由的组合暗示了“连续形而上学”（metafisica continua）的理念。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": Santo）则贡献了未曾展示的作品以完善展览项目。展览动线始于与阿尔贝托·萨维尼奥（Alberto Savinio）、费利切·卡索拉蒂（Felice Casorati）、卢西亚诺·法布罗（Luciano Fabro）、朱利奥·保利尼（Giulio Paolini）、萨尔沃（Salvo）和维弗雷多·拉姆（Wifredo "C馆举办两场展览。亚历山德罗·布尔吉尼（Alessandro Bulgini）的装置作品《永无乡加沙》（Neverland Gaza）上演了一场想象中的仪式，其灵感来自于斋月期间加沙废墟中共享茶水的举动。在这个悬置且放下武器的语境中，艺术成为一个可居住的、真实的、深深属于我们的空间。埃及艺术家亚历山大·穆斯塔法·法扎里（Alexander Mostafa Fazari）带来了装置作品《同情》（Compassione），其中一张紧急保温毯化作了艺术材料，艺术家的手则以书法笔触勾勒出纪伯伦、鲁米和伊本·阿拉比的词句。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "B馆则举办《活的歌剧，宣言——米兰壁垒 2015-2024》（Opera Viva, il Manifesto – Il punto di partenza è un’istantanea d’archivio, una vecchia fotografia, un volto, un paio di scarpe. article_text:
In occasione dell’edizione 2026 di Artissima , che aprirà al pubblico dal 30 ottobre al 1° novembre, Untitled Association vi accompagna alla scoperta di mostre, eventi e iniziative da non perdere nei giorni della Torino Art Week , con itinerari pensati per professionisti del settore, appassionati d’arte o semplici curiosi, tra musei, spazi istituzionali, gallerie private e spazi indipendenti.

Si comincia in centro storico, a pochi passi da Corso Regina Margherita con Luce Gallery , e Febo e Dafne , proseguiamo con Recontemporary e la nuova sede di Ciaccia Levi . Ci spostiamo verso via Po per visitare l’ Accademia Albertina di Belle Arti e Palazzo Madama . Si continua in zona Quadrilatero con la galleria Mazzoleni e, a pochi passi da Porta Nuova, A Pick Gallery . Concludiamo tra Borgo Crimea, con la Flashback Art Fair 2026 , e le nuove mostre al Museo Nazionale dell’ Automobile .

Torino Art Week 2026: gli appuntamenti di oggi

Negli spazi di Luce Gallery inaugura oggi Basta Giocare , la nuova personale dedicata all’artista Francesco Pirazzi . L’artista invita l’osservatore ad attraversare territori incerti, a riscoprire l’enigmatico nella semplicità. Il suo lavoro ci ricorda che il mondo non ha perso il proprio mistero; forse, semplicemente, ci siamo abituati ad esso.

Poco distante, anche la galleria Febo e Dafne presenta una nuova mostra dal titolo Invisibile meraviglia. Il disegno nascosto della natura , a cura di Massimo Ghirardini . Si tratta di una doppia personale degli artisti Massimo Barlettani , italiano, e Karina Chechik , argentina.

Dalla bellezza effimera di una fioritura fino ad una impenetrabile distesa di bambù, i due artisti indagano sul misterioso disegno di madre natura. Guidati dai riflessi della luce le loro opere ci inducono ad andare oltre la forma per immergerci nel labirintico percorso dei nostri mondi interiori. I disegni di fiori di Massimo Barlettani sono frutto di una ricerca sull’invisibile, sulle vibrazioni e l’energia che collega gli esseri viventi. Karina Chechik invita, tramite le sue immagini, l’osservatore a perdersi nella complessa esperienza del viandante.

Poco distante, a Largo Montebello, è visibile la Luce d’Artista Ice Cream Light di Vanessa Safavi . Essa consiste in cinquantaquattro sagome al neon che raffigurano coni gelato variopinti, che l’artista ha utilizzato come catalizzatori di alcuni stereotipi positivi legati all’immagine dell’Italia e al suo estro, come terra di buona cucina.

Proseguiamo verso Recontemporary, con le mostre Hikikomori di Megan Volpe e THE MAELSTRÖ M , di Santiago Sierra . Hikikomori è un’installazione della videoartista Megan Volpe, che riprende il termine giapponese utilizzato per descrivere il progressivo ritrarsi dal mondo esterno e la costruzione, fisica e mentale, di uno spazio nel quale protezione e isolamento finiscono per confondersi in una realtà mediata dalla tecnologia e dagli schermi. L’ambiente assume le forme di una sorta di paesaggio mentale, in cui tubi bianchi invadono l’architettura creando una ramificazione simile a quella del cervello.

L’opera video presentata da Santiago Sierra, realizzata nel 2023, è una registrazione di movimenti costruita a partire dalle posture di immobilizzazione imposte dalla polizia durante un arresto. I volti e i corpi non sono mai visibili e diventano sagome anonime, sottolineando i meccanismi attraverso i quali il potere disciplina, separa e determina la possibilità stessa di muoversi.

Segnaliamo inoltre, a pochi passi, la recente apertura della nuova sede torinese di Ciaccia Levi, galleria parigina, che dopo la chiusura dello spazio di Milano sceglie l’attico della Bottega d’Erasmo in via Gaudenzio Ferrari a Torino.

Ci spostiamo oltre via Po per visitare le mostre presso l’Accademia Albertina di Belle Arti e Palazzo Madama.

In occasione di Luci d’Artista, all’interno della sezione Costellazione , l’Accademia Albertina di Belle Arti riaccende sulla propria facciata Stelle danzanti , l’opera luminosa di Christian Grasso e Federico Prato . L’opera rilegge il capolavoro La Danse di Henri Matisse alla luce dell’immaginario visivo e poetico di Hayao Miyazaki, e individua nella danza un simbolo di unità e condivisione.

All’interno degli spazi dell’Accademia Albertina una mostra che presenta i risultati del 69° World Press Photo Contest, il prestigioso concorso internazionale del fotogiornalismo mondiale. Ogni anno il concorso premia i migliori fotografi professionisti e documentaristi che, attraverso immagini di straordinaria forza narrativa, raccontano gli eventi, le sfide e le trasformazioni che hanno segnato l’anno precedente. Sono esposte oltre 140 fotografie realizzate dai 42 autori premiati dalle giurie.

A Palazzo Madama è in mostra Il corpo della città. Moda e arti tra Liberty o modernità 1884.1961 , propone un punto di vista originale attraverso il quale osservare l’evolversi della città di Torino attraverso il corpo, inteso non soltanto come soggetto artistico, ma come spazio in cui si riflettono i cambiamenti sociali, economici e culturali, luogo ideale di intersezione fra moda, arte e trasformazioni urbane. Il percorso espositivo porta il visitatore in un percorso scandito dalle grandi Esposizioni tra XIX e XX secolo.

La mostra Giardini. L’arte di vivere la natura nel Settecento , curata da Clelia Arnaldi di Balme , accompagna il pubblico in un viaggio tra disegni, incisioni, tavole botaniche e progetti d’architettura dedicati all’arte del giardino nel XVIII secolo. La Sala Tessuti presenta inoltre Bianco al femminile , un percorso che racconta il legame tra il colore bianco, i tessuti e la storia delle donne attraverso cinquanta opere tessili di diversa lavorazione in un viaggio che attraversa sette secoli e valorizza il ruolo delle donne come creatrici, committenti, custodi di saperi e protagoniste di una tradizione.

Ricordiamo la prossima apertura, prevista per martedì 17 novembre, intitolata L ’enigma del sorriso , dedicata ad Antonello da Messina e alla trasformazione del ritratto come luogo di costruzione dell’identità moderna.

In zona Quadrilatero la galleria Mazzoleni di Torino inaugura la mostra Giorgio de Chirico. Enigma contemporaneo , presentando un artista centrale nella storia collezionistica della famiglia e della programmazione della galleria. Le opere di de Chirico sono poste in dialogo con una selezione di opere di artisti storicizzati e contemporanei che, in modi diversi, ne hanno raccolto l’eredità secondo accostamenti liberi, che suggeriscono l’idea di una “metafisica continua”.

La mostra si è sviluppata attraverso un dialogo diretto con gli artisti coinvolti e con la disponibilità degli archivi e delle fondazioni di riferimento. Nunzio, Paolini e Senatore hanno realizzato nuove opere per l’occasione; Francolino e Astore hanno curato l’allestimento site-specific dei loro lavori; mentre do Esp í rito Santo ha concesso opere inedite a completamento del progetto espositivo. Il percorso prende avvio dai dialoghi con Alberto Savinio, Felice Casorati, Luciano Fabro, Giulio Paolini, Salvo e Wifredo Lam , ricostruendo una genealogia di artisti che hanno interrogato, ciascuno secondo il proprio stile, il tema del mito, della classicità e della metamorfosi.

Proseguiamo verso Porta Nuova, con una delle installazioni all’interno del programma di Luci d’Artista. Con Scia’Mano , al Giardino Sambuy, Luigi Ontani realizza una apparizione sciamanica sotto forma di stampa lenticolare. Il lightbox bifacciale, posizionato di fronte alla sede storica della libreria e casa editrice Fogola, è un tributo alla tradizione magica della città di Torino.

In via Galliari A Pick Gallery inaugura due nuove mostre. La prima, The Gender of Images , è la personale dedicata a Tonino Lacertosa , che riflette sul tema della memoria e sulla trasformazione dei frammenti visivi. Il punto di partenza è un’istantanea d’archivio, una vecchia fotografia, un volto, un paio di scarpe. Questo materiale si deposita sulla tela, consegnato alla lentezza della stesura, dove la fonte iniziale persiste come un’eco distante. Le immagini non si esauriscono nella loro apparizione e attendono di essere riattivate dallo sguardo.

La seconda mostra, The Insiders , è un affondo sulla produzione pittorica dell’artista cinese SunJing . Il corpo è considerato come un paesaggio modellato da emozioni, dall’ambiente e dai condizionamenti sociali. Le figure rappresentate non sono ritratti in senso tradizionale, sono attraversate e definite dal desiderio, dall’ansia, vulnerabilità o stanchezza; elementi caratterizzati anche dalla tensione materica delle tele. SunJing definisce tale approccio una forma di “realismo psicologico”.

Nei paraggi, negli spazi dell’ex-Tuxedo in via Belfiore, segnaliamo la Galleria Umberto Benappi e la collettiva Join Us in the Underground che da domani riunirà per tre giorni nei nuovi spazi della galleria un articolato gruppo di artisti appartenenti a generazioni e ricerche differenti: Maurizio Bertinetti , Maurizio Camerani, Gianni Dess ì , Francesca Dondoglio , Carlo D ’ Oria , Giuseppe Gallo , Aldo Mondino, Frederique Nalbandian , Paolo Pellegrin , Michelangelo Pistoletto , Julian Schnabel, Guendalina Urbani, Nunzio e Marzio Zorio . La mostra sarà visitabile solo dal 29 ottobre al primo novembre, in concomitanza con Artissima e con la Torino Art Week. Vi ricordiamo inoltre, il 31 ottobre in occasione della Notte delle Arti Contemporanee di TAG – Torino Art Galleries, l’apertura straordinaria della galleria dalle ore 18 alle ore 23.

In zona Borgo Crimea oggi inaugura l’anteprima di Flashback Art Fair, giunta alla sua ventiquattresima edizione, con il titolo IN TIME . Negli spazi di Flashback Habitat (il centro indipendente per le culture contemporanee con sede a Torino in corso Lanza 75 diretto dall’artista Alessandro Bulgini ) rinasce Flashback, l’arte è tutta contemporanea , la fiera diretta da Stefania Poddighe e Ginevra Pucci . IN TIME è un nuovo capitolo che prosegue la ricerca sul tempo come dimensione aperta, nella quale passato, presente e futuro convivono e si trasformano reciprocamente.

Per l’edizione 2026, Flashback invita le gallerie ospiti a proporre lavori capaci di interrogare il presente, riconoscendo nella memoria una materia viva. Opere di secoli diversi entrano in relazione, aprono domande e acquistano nuovi significati nell’incontro con chi le osserva. Flashback Art Fair inaugurerà al pubblico nella giornata di domani 29 ottobre 2026.

Due le mostre al Padiglione C. Neverland Gaza , installazione di Alessandro Bulgini , che mette in scena un rito immaginario, ispirato al gesto del tè condiviso tra le macerie di Gaza durante il Ramadan. In questo contesto sospeso e disarmato, l’arte si fa spazio abitabile, reale, profondamente nostro. L’artista egiziano Alexander Mostafa Fazari presenta l’installazione Compassione , in cui una coperta termica d’emergenza si fa materiale artistico e la mano dell’artista traccia con il segno calligrafico le parole di Gibran, Rumi e Ibn Arabi.

Il Padiglione B ospita invece Opera Viva, il Manifesto – Barriera di Milano 2015-2024 , una raccolta delle immagini delle edizioni precedenti del progetto sul territorio a cura di Alessandro Bulgini. Troviamo poi Unconscious Elevation , opera installativa di Carl von Pfeil in bilico tra ascesa e discesa esistenziale. Un ascensore ci immerge fisicamente nell’opera, dove un’elegia sonora progressiva ci guida verso soglie interiori.

Installata sul tetto del Padiglione C, è visibile la Luce d’artista mater , realizzata da Alessandro Bulgini e dedicata a coloro che sono nati nell’ex brefotrofio della Provincia di Torino, oggi gestito dall’Associazione Flashback.

Segnaliamo inoltre l’edizione 2026 di Opera Viva, Il Manifesto – IN TIME , in Piazza Bottesini, incentrata sui temi del viaggio e della navigazione, a partire dalla simbologia della barca a vela e del Bucintoro dei Savoia, fino agli attraversamenti del Mediterraneo da parte della Global Sumud Flotilla. Pur accostando esperienze storicamente lontane, il Bucintoro riconosce il valore di chi ha scelto di mettersi in viaggio e di vivere il mare non come confine, ma come spazio in cui rendere visibile una responsabilità collettiva. Un’immagine nata per celebrare l’autorità diventa così strumento di riflessione sul presente.

Concludiamo l’itinerario di oggi con la segnalazione di un’inaugurazione fuori dal percorso. Il MAUTO – Museo Nazionale dell’Automobile, presenta due nuove mostre nella sua sede di Corso Unità d’Italia 40. La prima, Serie Limitata. Paesaggi mobili in fotografia , a cura di Lorenza Bravetta e Philippe S écler offre un panorama completo di scatti fotografici, video e sculture riunendo il lavoro di quaranta artisti da Eugène Atget alle più recenti esperienze della post-fotografia. Al centro della mostra è l’automobile come protagonista della cultura visiva degli ultimi centocinquanta anni.

Negli spazi della Project Room troviamo Gerald Laing. Full Speed , a cura di Elena Geuna , realizzata in collaborazione con The Estate of Gerald Laing. Figura di spicco della Pop Art inglese, Laing è stato uno degli artisti che meglio hanno interpretato il rapporto tra arte, velocità, tecnologia e cultura dell’immagine. La mostra propone una rilettura della pratica artistica di Laing con opere dal forte impatto visivo, molte delle quali mai esposte prima in Italia.

article_text:
Films and events

Galas

Prima Facie

Oscar nominee Cynthia Erivo gives a captivating central performance in Susanna White’s much-anticipated screen adaptation of Suzie Miller’s globally acclaimed play.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director Susanna White

Screenwriter Suzie Miller

With Cynthia Erivo, Daniel Ings, Toheeb Jimoh, Noma Dumezweni, Elliot Levey

UK-Australia 2026. 106min

Courtesy of Sony Pictures Releasing UK

Language English

Access information

Tuesday 13 October 21:15

Audio description

Closed Captions (CC) via WatchWord smart glasses

Friday 16 October 20:50

Audio description

Descriptive subtitles

Saturday 17 October 11:00

Audio description

Descriptive subtitles

Find out about booking access tickets

Introduction

Tessa is an ambitious barrister, used to winning and dominating in the courtroom by defending men accused of sexual assault. But when she unexpectedly becomes the accuser in a sexual assault case, she is forced to confront the legal system that she once trusted. This is a powerful exploration of a woman’s fight for justice and the power dynamics at play in a patriarchal world.

Isabel Moir

Content advice

Contains scenes of sex and sexual violence.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

Screen Talk: Cynthia Erivo

As she prepares to unveil her mesmerising performance in Prima Facie, we welcome Cynthia Erivo to this Screen Talk.

The Debut

For LFF 2026’s curtain call, writer-director Jesse Eisenberg delivers a rapturous and raucously funny love letter to community theatre, featuring a luminous lead performance by Julianne Moore.

Frank and Percy

Roger Allam and Ian McKellen excel as the titular characters in this adaptation of the West End hit, about finding connection beyond your sixties.

Hace un año me lancé en la aventura de entender su complejidad desde la subjetividad que me caracteriza; amo pensar en él como un homosexual flamboyán y tropical, que fabrica metáforas y revueltas desde el corazón de la modernidad. Es exactamente desde esa imagen que fue pensado el guion curatorial de su última muestra en París. Concebido como un proyecto conjunto entre las galerías Mountains y Baró , la idea era desmontar el mito que lo ubica como un pionero del arte cinético, para acercarlo a la imagen de un poeta dadaísta que nunca tuvo miedo de celebrar el amor homosexual y pensar su obra como archipiélago de conexiones improbables.", "links": [{"text": "Baró", "url": "https://barogaleria.com/exhibitions/217-le-desir-cinetique...-david-medalla/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sobre máquinas de espuma y estéticas generativas"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Frente a la infinitud de una obra generativa, los amantes de la pintura moderna no siempre tienen herramientas para descifrar su belleza. David Medalla (Manila, Filipinas,1942-2020) encontró la forma para envolvernos en este universo, convirtiendo su amor por la naturaleza y el inconsciente humano en sutiles máquinas que evolucionan como un sueño infinito incrustado en nuestro iris."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "En 1961 Medalla fue llamado por Metzger “the master of auto créatif art”, gracias a sus icónicas series de esculturas Cloud Canyons o Bubble machines . Estas esculturas vivas, asociadas por la crítica de la época a las preocupaciones en torno al movimiento cinético, no son otra cosa que un silencioso gesto de alquimia donde la materia es transformada en energía, gracias a una reacción química que da vida a organismos que evolucionan sin parar, como burbujas, desde el corazón de torres cilíndricas o rectangulares."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Esta poética anticipa conceptos hiper contemporáneos todavía ajenos para el gran público como arte generativo, o incluso el concepto de bioarte introducido por Eduardo Kac en 1999, al convertir la manipulación genética en una forma de arte.", "links": [{"text": "Eduardo Kac", "url": "https://artishockrevista.com/tag/eduardo-kac/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Eso que conocemos hoy como arte generativo asociado a la IA nació en los años cincuenta como un periodo de transición, donde la materialidad del arte concreto se transformaba en enjambres de píxeles y permutaciones que se mueven en coreografías interminables pautadas por cálculos matemáticos."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sí, Medalla estaba en el centro de ese huracán gracias a su vínculo con una de las biblias del avant-garde cinético, la revista SIGNALS (agosto,1964 – marzo, 1966), pero él tenía su alma en otro lugar. Mientras gran parte de los artistas cinéticos buscaban el movimiento y la imagen infinita en un estudio profundo de la geometría con permutaciones de color o intensos estudios numerológicos para modelar el vacío, Medalla, con humor, nos recuerda que la vida cotidiana existe."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artishockrevista.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/David-Medalla-Le-Desir-Cinetique.-exhibition-views-Baro-Paris-C-Hafid-Lhachmi-ADAGP-Paris-2026.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Vista de la exposición David Medalla: Le Désir Cinétique… en galería Baró, París, 2026. article_text:
Escultor, performer, agitador del absurdo y poeta, David Medalla es uno de los personajes más poliédricos del arte de posguerra. Hace un año me lancé en la aventura de entender su complejidad desde la subjetividad que me caracteriza; amo pensar en él como un homosexual flamboyán y tropical, que fabrica metáforas y revueltas desde el corazón de la modernidad. Es exactamente desde esa imagen que fue pensado el guion curatorial de su última muestra en París. Concebido como un proyecto conjunto entre las galerías Mountains y Baró , la idea era desmontar el mito que lo ubica como un pionero del arte cinético, para acercarlo a la imagen de un poeta dadaísta que nunca tuvo miedo de celebrar el amor homosexual y pensar su obra como archipiélago de conexiones improbables.

Sobre máquinas de espuma y estéticas generativas

Frente a la infinitud de una obra generativa, los amantes de la pintura moderna no siempre tienen herramientas para descifrar su belleza. David Medalla (Manila, Filipinas,1942-2020) encontró la forma para envolvernos en este universo, convirtiendo su amor por la naturaleza y el inconsciente humano en sutiles máquinas que evolucionan como un sueño infinito incrustado en nuestro iris.

En 1961 Medalla fue llamado por Metzger “the master of auto créatif art”, gracias a sus icónicas series de esculturas Cloud Canyons o Bubble machines . Estas esculturas vivas, asociadas por la crítica de la época a las preocupaciones en torno al movimiento cinético, no son otra cosa que un silencioso gesto de alquimia donde la materia es transformada en energía, gracias a una reacción química que da vida a organismos que evolucionan sin parar, como burbujas, desde el corazón de torres cilíndricas o rectangulares.

Esta poética anticipa conceptos hiper contemporáneos todavía ajenos para el gran público como arte generativo, o incluso el concepto de bioarte introducido por Eduardo Kac en 1999, al convertir la manipulación genética en una forma de arte.

Eso que conocemos hoy como arte generativo asociado a la IA nació en los años cincuenta como un periodo de transición, donde la materialidad del arte concreto se transformaba en enjambres de píxeles y permutaciones que se mueven en coreografías interminables pautadas por cálculos matemáticos.

Sí, Medalla estaba en el centro de ese huracán gracias a su vínculo con una de las biblias del avant-garde cinético, la revista SIGNALS (agosto,1964 – marzo, 1966), pero él tenía su alma en otro lugar. Mientras gran parte de los artistas cinéticos buscaban el movimiento y la imagen infinita en un estudio profundo de la geometría con permutaciones de color o intensos estudios numerológicos para modelar el vacío, Medalla, con humor, nos recuerda que la vida cotidiana existe.

Medalla crea metáforas delirantes, como la leche de coco preparada por su madre o la espuma en la boca de un combatiente moribundo bajo los golpes de los ocupantes japoneses, referentes históricos como La nube en pantalones de Maiakovski y, por qué no, un gran falo disparando amor. Sus obras son todo eso y más, postura que quizás lo ubica en un punto más cercano al dadaísmo que al cinetismo (no fue por azar que Marcel Duchamp le dedicó una obra en 1964: Bouche-évier [Tapón de desagüe o de fregadero]).

Las Bubbles Machines marcaron una superación del minimalismo y un primer paso hacia el Biocinetismo , que el artista continuaría explorando con la arena y el barro en series posteriores. Él afirmaba haber buscado para la escultura el equivalente a lo que la célula representa para el organismo: una materia capaz de multiplicarse.

Actualmente existen once versiones de esta serie, que cambian según la cantidad de tubos, desde la primera y sencilla versión en cinco cajas, hasta las muy complejas realizadas en plexiglás, portales alegóricos a Mondrian que se debaten entre movimiento, quietud, caos y orden; o, como dijo Guy Brett, «algo material y una nada inmaterial». En la muestra tuvimos la oportunidad de presentar dos.

Nací en Manila —ciudad que quedó totalmente arrasada por los bombardeos durante la guerra […] crecí pensando que la nueva tecnología servía para destruir. Pero la nueva tecnología también llegó para reconstruir. Luego, muy pronto, viajé a Estados Unidos y descubrí dos tipos de culturas: una altamente tecnológica y desarrollada, y otra donde la naturaleza se encontraba en estado puro. Me interesaban profundamente la naturaleza y el ser humano, y entre ambos estaba la máquina .

D.M

SIGNALS y la modernidad tropical

En agosto de 1964, el crítico de arte Guy Brett, Paul Keeler y los artistas Gustav Metzger, Marcello Salvadori y David Medalla comenzaron a publicar el Signals Newsbulletin como parte del Centre for Advanced Creative Study (Centro de Estudios Creativos Avanzados), que habían establecido en el apartamento compartido por Medalla y Keeler en Cornwall Gardens, South Kensington. Esta publicación, editada por Medalla y con formato de periódico, tomó su nombre de la serie de esculturas de tensión Signals —iniciada en 1955— del artista griego Takis .

Con un énfasis particular en el arte cinético y en la obra de artistas de América Latina, ellos proponen un foro para todos aquellos que soñaban con la integración imaginativa del arte con la tecnología, la ciencia, la arquitectura y nuestro entorno en su totalidad. Signals también fue una galería en funcionamiento desde noviembre de 1964 hasta septiembre de 1966 en estrecha relación con los principales colectivos conformados por artistas latinoamericanos, como los argentinos de GRAV , los brasileños del movimiento neoconcreto y los venezolanos herederos del colectivo Los Disidentes .

Eso fue lo que le permitió orquestar otra visión de la modernidad pensada desde el sur e impulsada por las investigaciones de artistas como Hélio Oiticica , Lygia Clark y Jesús Rafael Soto , quienes se alejan de la lógica cartesiana y la dureza de la tecnología para repensar la abstracción y el cinetismo desde lo sensorial, lo artesanal e, incluso, lo emocional, forjando una nueva escultura que crece de forma aleatoria e imprevista, más cercana a la evolución rizomática del paisaje tropical que al movimiento de la máquina tan celebrado por artistas desde el futurismo.

Medalla se sentía muy cercano al movimiento neoconcreto de Brasil, en especial a Clark y Oiticica, como lo atestiguan las cartas presentes en la muestra. De hecho, podría decir que hay una sensibilidad en torno a la fiesta popular, la noción de obra colectiva e incluso su capacidad de erotizar la geometría.

Estas investigaciones expresan una postura muy particular frente a la modernidad. Podríamos hablar incluso de un camino inverso al de la utopía moderna, que en lugar de celebrar la mecanización y el progreso tecnológico, reivindica lo artesanal y, por qué no, el manejo erótico de la materia. Estas revueltas estéticas surgen en el clímax de los llamados treinta gloriosos , un periodo de gran optimismo tecnológico en la Europa de posguerra, marcado por la fascinación ante los avances científicos, los nuevos medios de transporte y comunicación, y la expectativa de la conquista del espacio. Muchos artistas veían en la máquina una promesa de futuro. Medalla, en cambio, intentaba resaltar la coexistencia de la máquina y la naturaleza, una postura que él llamaba “realismo sinóptico”.

Mientras el arte cinético defendía el rechazo a cualquier referente narrativo, literario o anecdótico, y la desvinculación de la obra de arte con respecto a su creador, Medalla nunca abandonó la figuración y apostaba por situaciones delirantes que lanzan anzuelos al inconsciente, y a una pintura figurativa de trazos bruscos y lúdicos que ilustraban su amor por la vida cotidiana.

Él se definía como nómada, operando con un modelo de pensamiento casi archipelágico, donde múltiples capas de sentido y referentes culturales podrían coexistir. Esta visión global y casi creole de la cultura podemos verla en sus experiencias interactivas, donde el público es invitado a coser, y en algunos de los colectivos que fundó, como Artists for Democracy (Artistas por la Democracia), The Exploding Galaxy (La Galaxia Explosiva), The Artists Liberation Front (Frente de Liberación de los Artistas) y Baroque Buddha Brotherhood (Hermandad del Buda Barroco).

Amor marica y torbellino moderno

Para David Medalla, Mondrian fue mucho más que uno de los grandes nombres de la abstracción geométrica. Desde muy joven se dejó impregnar e inspirar por su universo, pero también se obsesionó con una idea: apropiarse de esa abstracción desde la mirada de un maricón tropical.

En 1992, junto al artista australiano Adam Nankervis , su pareja y colaborador, fundó en Nueva York el Mondrian Fan Club , una extensión de los anteriores Flying Mondrians de Medalla. En cada ciudad donde se reunían —desde Berlín y Ámsterdam hasta Roma y Río—, el dúo llevaba a cabo acciones y fotografiaba una «letra», componiendo poco a poco una frase en homenaje a Piet Mondrian, llevando su imaginario desde el espacio tradicional de la pintura hacia situaciones participativas y cargadas de humor.

En Mondrian in Excelsis , por ejemplo, una fotografía muestra a un hombre vistiendo un traje de baño estampado con sus características líneas y colores primarios. La modernidad se da el permiso de viajar al trópico, entre humor y provocación.

Proyectar a Mondrian sobre el cuerpo mulato de las favelas es desplazar el lenguaje de la abstracción de su lugar de autoridad y devolverlo al mundo de lo cotidiano, del deseo, del humor y de la experiencia corporal. Esta imagen no destruye el ícono de la abstracción: quizás llevar la abstracción al deseo sea también una forma de llevarlo a la vida.

A Stitch in Time comenzó en 1968; tenía dos amantes que, por casualidad, llegaron a Londres al mismo tiempo. Uno regresaba a California y el otro iba a la India, y en aquella época las esperas en los aeropuertos eran aún más largas. Tenía que verlos a ambos en el mismo lugar y no tenía nada que regalarles. Tenía dos pañuelos —así fue como empezó todo— y algo de aguja e hilo; por cierto, se me da muy mal coser, ni siquiera sabía pegar un botón. Así que les dije: «Oigan, por si se aburren durante el viaje, ¿por qué no se ponen a coser cosas?». Entiendo que hacer labores de costura resulta muy terapéutico y hace que la espera de los vuelos sea menos aburrida. Les di un pañuelo a cada uno; al principio, yo mismo bordé mi nombre, la fecha, la palabra «amor» y todo eso. No volví a verlos —ni a los amantes ni a los pañuelos.

D.M

Medalla nunca dudó en arrojar luz sobre su deseo, y sobre los iconos de la erudición homosexual, como García Lorca o Hélio Oiticica, a quien dedicó una obra (aun sin conocerlo). También dedicó decenas de obras a sus compañeros de vida. Algunas obras de esta exposición nos lo recuerdan desde una postura lúdica y diáfana en distintos momentos de su vida, donde incluso la pornografía puede ser transformada en performatividad y experiencia lúdica. Conscientes de ello, como un ejercicio de revisión histórica, los invito a darnos permiso de celebrar esta imagen fálica que dispara una galaxia de vida y espuma frente al retrato de un amante, preguntándonos: ¿Hasta qué punto es posible erotizar una máquina?

*En el marco de la muestra se realizó una jornada de estudio con estudiantes de la Sorbonne, así como la performance Looking for Medalla! , a cargo del artista venezolano Luis Salazar . Inspirado en la obra de David Medalla, Salazar asumió el papel de poeta experimental para imaginar una trama delirante entre Mondrian, Medalla, Lygia Clark y Hélio Oiticica. Mediante carteles de amor y odio y una combinación de materiales tan disímiles como sacos de yute, espuma, rollos de hilo y chocolate, junto con referencias a la herencia de la Bauhaus, construyó una escena tan lúdica como provocadora. Lejos de ser un gesto superficial o meramente sarcástico, la performance proponía una revisión crítica de la historia del arte moderno y de las relaciones de poder que han definido sus centros y periferias.

article_text:
Jenny Holzer über die Aufstände in Frankreich, Düsseldorfer und Kölner Galerien protestieren gegen AfD-Veranstaltung – und ein beschwingter Previewtag der Art Basel Paris: Das ist unsere Medienschau am Mittwoch

Debatte

In der WDR-Sendung "Westart" berichtet Galeristin Daniela Steinfeld über den Protest Düsseldorfer und Kölner Galerien gegen eine geplante AfD-Veranstaltung zur Kulturpolitik von rechts. Steinfeld, Mitinitiatorin eines offenen Briefs , kritisiert den Versuch, Heinrich Heine und Joseph Beuys für einen völkischen Kulturbegriff zu vereinnahmen. "Aus einem Patrioten wird dann ganz schnell ein Völkischer", warnt sie. Die AfD wolle den Kunst- und Kulturbegriff kapern und letztlich eine deutsche, völkische Kunst definieren. Dem setzt Steinfeld die Freiheit künstlerischer Produktion entgegen: Kunst müsse sämtliche Ausdrucksformen zulassen, auch unbequeme und gesellschaftskritische. Keine Partei dürfe bestimmen, was Kunst sei. Das gelte auch für den Umgang mit demokratiefeindlichen Kräften: "Selbst die Feinde der Demokratie dürfen sich äußern. Aber wir dürfen uns halt auch äußern."

Jenny Holzer geht im "T"-Magazin der "New York Times" anlässlich ihrer Ausstellung im Pariser Musée d’Orsay auch auf die Proteste junger Menschen in Frankreich ein. Die US-amerikanische Künstlerin findet es "grausam, dass Kinder für eine bessere Bildung kämpfen müssen", für angemessen bezahlte Lehrkräfte und saubere Schulen. Zugleich sorge sie sich um die Sicherheit der Jugendlichen. Die Proteste, an denen Hunderttausende gegen ungleiche Bildungschancen auf die Straße gehen, stehen für Holzer im Zusammenhang mit einer umfassenderen Krise. Auf die Frage, was sie an der Gegenwart besonders verstöre, nennt sie Kriege, Hunger, Flucht, die Klimakrise und die Konzentration von Reichtum. Ihre Ausstellung versammelt historische Stimmen, deren Aussagen erstaunlich aktuell wirkten. Als Botschaft an das Publikum formuliert Holzer dennoch einen vorsichtigen Appell: "Gebt noch nicht auf."

Kunstmarkt

Andrew Russeth berichtet auf "Artnet News" von einem schwungvollen Auftakt der Art Basel Paris mit hochpreisigen Angeboten und ersten Millionenverkäufen. Im Grand Palais wird ein Akt von Amedeo Modigliani aus dem Jahr 1917 für mehr als 100 Millionen Dollar angeboten. Hauser & Wirth verkauft einen Gerhard Richter für rund zehn Millionen Dollar, Gagosian meldet den Verkauf eines späten Willem de Kooning im achtstelligen Bereich. Russeth beobachtet eine ausgelassene Stimmung unter den Händlern und sieht Paris im Aufstieg zur vielleicht wichtigsten Ausgabe der Art-Basel-Messen: "Alle sagen inzwischen, dass Paris-Basel mit Basel gleichgezogen hat", schreibt er. Vielleicht habe die französische Hauptstadt das Schweizer Original "sogar übertroffen." Neben den großen Namen hebt er junge Galerien hervor, darunter die Seouler Galerie P21 mit verstörenden Skulpturen von Haneyl Choi. Die Messe vereine Marktmacht und Entdeckungen.

KI

Bei "Hyperallergic" kritisiert Valentina Di Liscia den zunehmenden Einsatz generativer KI in der Kunstwelt . Während Künstlerinnen und Künstler KI oft nutzten, um angesichts unbezahlter Kommunikationsarbeit Zeit für ihre eigentliche Praxis zu bewahren, hätten finanzstarke Museen, Stiftungen und Kulturorganisationen keine Entschuldigung dafür, auf Kosten professioneller Autorinnen und Autoren Pressetexte, Wandbeschriftungen und Künstlerstatements automatisieren zu lassen. KI-Texte seien häufig stilistisch selbstbewusst, inhaltlich aber hohl. Zudem reproduziere die Technologie die Arbeit anderer, ohne diese angemessen anzuerkennen oder zu vergüten. Di Liscia warnt vor einer weiteren Entwertung kultureller Arbeit und dem Verlust gedanklicher Tiefe: Kunstinstitutionen schuldeten ihrem Publikum eine Sprache, die echte Bedeutung erschließe. Ihr Fazit: "Und ja, liebe Kunstwelt: Wir merken es."

Der Schweizer Bestsellerautor Martin Suter hingegen fürchtet nicht um die Literatur . "Die KI kann einen Liebesroman schreiben, aber sie kann nicht fühlen, wie es ist, verliebt zu sein", sagt Suter der dpa. "Ich glaube, das ist unser Trumpf im Ärmel. Wir fühlen die Gefühle, die wir beschreiben. Und das, wenn man ein bisschen sensibel ist, merkt man beim Lesen." Suter betont den Unterschied zwischen Wissen und Intelligenz. "Wir merken doch den Unterschied zwischen einem Menschen, der Wissen hat, also der viel gelernt hat, und einem intelligenten Menschen. Das ist meine Hoffnung, dass wir diesen Unterschied auch in Zukunft spüren." Ein Freund habe ihm einmal ein paar Seiten zugeschickt, die er von einer KI "im Stil von Martin Suter" erstellen ließ. Das Ergebnis habe ihn sehr beruhigt, sagt Suter - das sei mit seinen Texten nicht zu verwechseln gewesen. Es sieht aber ein Problem: Im Laufe der Zeit dürften immer weniger Leute merken, wenn etwas nicht echt ist, "denn man gewöhnt sich ja an diese Art". Suters neuer Roman "Ein und Alles" kommt am 21. Oktober heraus – selbst geschrieben, wie er betont.
